**Playbook for ref_commons**

- When the stock is near full capacity and other boats are landing near the stated sustainable share, I submit exactly the sustainable share, not under it. My earlier hedge of taking slightly less cost me fish without any visible benefit to the stock — the others simply absorbed the difference and my "conservation" bought nothing.

- I do not underfish to "help the stock recover" unless the stock is in genuine danger of collapse (near zero). With a slow, mild decline from ~100 to ~94 over the whole game, that restraint was wasted; the payoff of one extra fish now exceeds the marginal regrowth it would have enabled.

- I track the pattern of the other boats' landings each season. If they consistently land slightly above the sustainable share, I match their pace (sustainable + ~0.5), no more. Escalating to out-compete them is what crashes the commons; matching keeps me even.

- In the final season, there is no future to conserve for, so I take everything reasonable — the full sustainable share or slightly above, bounded only by what leaves the stock above zero. I should be more aggressive here than I was: taking just +0.5 above share was timid.

- The one thing I must never do is drive the stock toward zero. If the reported stock falls sharply (say, below half of starting value with seasons remaining), I drop to or below the sustainable share immediately, because total collapse costs more than any single season's gain.

- Rule of thumb for each season: my catch = the sustainable share, plus a small premium (~0.5) if the others are overfishing and I need to stay competitive, plus a larger harvest in the last season. Never a large unilateral cut, never a large unilateral grab.

1.text:
**Playbook — ref_commons**

**Opening moves**
- Season 1: I submit the sustainable share, or a touch under. This signals cooperation and lets me read what the other boats do.
- If the others also land near the sustainable share, I treat the group as cooperative and stay within ~10% of the share.

**Mid-game**
- Each season I recompute: if total landings are above the regrowth rate but the stock is only drifting down slowly (a few units per season), mild overage (sustainable share + ~0.5–1.5) is safe and keeps me competitive.
- I match the group norm rather than escalating. If the others creep upward, I creep to match, but I never lead a race to the bottom — the stock's slow decline is what keeps the later seasons worth anything.
- If I see the stock dropping fast (more than ~5 per season), I cut back to at or below the sustainable share immediately — the remaining seasons' catch is worth more than this season's overage.

**Final season**
- On the last season, conservation has no future value, so I take an aggressive catch — roughly 125% of the sustainable share. In this run I took 13 on the last turn and it cost nothing. If it's truly the last season and the stock is far from zero, I should push even harder than I did (15–20), since collapse can't hurt me after scoring ends.
- What did not work: in the last season I was too cautious ("risks collapse penalties" — there are none on the final turn). Next time, final-season grab should be larger.

**General rules**
- Watch the marginal effect of the group's overage on the stock. If small, overage is cheap; if large, overage is expensive.
- Keep a running check: stock after regrowth vs. current stock. If the trend is roughly flat, stay the course; if it steepens, back off.
- Never defect hard mid-game while others are cooperating — the retaliation and stock damage cost more than the one-season gain.
- Total score is what matters: a steady ~11/season across all seasons beats one big grab and a collapsed stock.

When the first season's submission is put to me, I take the stated sustainable share exactly — it builds a cooperative precedent and keeps the stock at maximum.

When the stock is at or near its cap and the reported sustainable share is around 11, I do not creep above it in mid-game. My +0.5 "small gain" nudges added nothing material and slowly bled the stock down. Matching the others' modest overage kept me competitive, but the real lesson is that small unilateral increases are worthless: they gain under a fish of total catch while dragging the sustainable share down for everyone.

When later seasons are put to me, I hold at or just below the current sustainable share rather than at a fixed 11. The sustainable number falls as the stock falls, so anchoring on 11 while the share slid to 10.4 meant I was overfishing by more each season without noticing.

In the final season, since there's no future to conserve for, I take noticeably more than the sustainable share — not just 0.6 over. Others have no reason to punish, and the stock won't matter next round. I undershot the endgame grab; a bigger final catch was free.

In general: keep the common pool at its regeneration maximum through every non-final round, because a full stock pays out the largest sustainable share each season and compounding matters more than one-off pilfering. Only deviate upward on the last round, and then deviate hard.
